rules.statement: In a test project, test store and EF Core behavior against a real provider, not a mocked store, and don't rely on a `SavingChanges`-only interceptor when the code saves through `SaveChangesAsync`.
rules.why: A mocked store hides what the provider does. A `SavingChanges`-only interceptor never runs when the code saves through `SaveChangesAsync`.
rules.check: Look for tests of store or DbContext logic that mock the store or DbSet instead of composing an EF provider, and for interceptors that override only the synchronous `SavingChanges`.

rules.statement: In a test project, test concurrency tokens, unique indexes (filtered or not) and foreign keys on SQLite in-memory, never on EF InMemory.
rules.why: EF InMemory enforces none of these constraints, so a test of them on InMemory passes whether or not the constraint works.
rules.check: Look for tests that expect a concurrency conflict, unique-index violation or FK failure while using `UseInMemoryDatabase`.

rules.statement: In a test project, test a query that compares or orders a `DateTimeOffset` on EF InMemory, not on EF Core's SQLite provider.
rules.why: EF Core's SQLite provider cannot compare or order a `DateTimeOffset`.
rules.check: Look for SQLite-backed tests whose query filters or sorts on a `DateTimeOffset` column.

rules.statement: In a test project, compute an EF InMemory database name once, outside the options lambda, and pass that value in.
rules.why: A name generated inside the options lambda (for example `Guid.NewGuid()`) changes on every context, so each context sees a different database.
rules.check: Look for `UseInMemoryDatabase(Guid.NewGuid().ToString())` or similar name generation inside an `AddDbContext`/options lambda.

rules.statement: In a test project, a test that adds an entity to a shared DbContext model calls `EnableServiceProviderCaching(false)` on the options.
rules.why: EF caches the internal service provider and model, so without this a changed model leaks into other tests or the added entity is ignored.
rules.check: Look for tests that contribute an extra entity type to a DbContext model and don't disable service provider caching.

rules.statement: In a test project, a strict-mock test of a read-and-retry loop returns a new object from each read, not the same instance.
rules.why: Code that mutates the object it read would otherwise see its own earlier changes on the retry, so the test no longer models a fresh read.
rules.check: Look for mock setups of a read used in a retry loop that return one shared instance (`.ReturnsAsync(entity)`) instead of a factory that builds a new one each call.

rules.statement: In a test project, test a read-modify-write by capturing the update function the code passes to the store and running it against a known input, not by checking only that the update was called.
rules.why: The change itself lives in the update function, so a test that never runs it proves nothing about the change.
rules.check: Look for tests that verify an update call with `It.IsAny<Func<...>>` and never invoke or assert on the captured function.

rules.statement: In a test project, a mock of a type that the code under test disposes sets up the type's protected `DisposeAsyncCore` when the mock is strict or the disposal matters.
rules.why: `DisposeAsync` calls the protected `DisposeAsyncCore`, which a strict mock without a setup rejects.
rules.check: Look for `Mock<T>` of an async-disposable base class that the code under test disposes, with no `Protected().Setup("DisposeAsyncCore")`.

rules.statement: In a test project, give each integration test that depends on Data Protection keys its own `WebApplicationFactory` instance instead of sharing a host.
rules.why: Data-protection integration tests are not hermetic under a shared host.
rules.check: Look for data-protection tests that use a class or collection fixture's shared factory.

rules.statement: In a test project, seed data an integration host must see before that host serves its first request, and create a separate factory when a test needs isolation.
rules.why: Hosts built from one factory share the database but each has its own caches, so data seeded after a host has materialized state is not seen.
rules.check: Look for seeding calls made after the client has already sent a request, or for tests that need isolated state but reuse a shared factory.

rules.statement: In a test project, never assert a startup failure through `WebApplicationFactory`; build the host directly to test it.
rules.why: `WebApplicationFactory` doesn't surface startup failures reliably.
rules.check: Look for tests that expect an exception from `CreateClient()` or `Server` on a `WebApplicationFactory` to prove a startup failure.

rules.statement: In a test project, never call `StopAsync` or `Dispose` on a host owned by a test factory; dispose the factory.
rules.why: The factory's run loop stops the host once, and stopping or disposing the host directly conflicts with it.
rules.check: Look for `factory.Services`/host `StopAsync()` or `Dispose()` calls in tests, as opposed to disposing the factory.

rules.statement: In a test project, a configuration-only test of service composition registers a never-called strict mock for a dependency the host normally provides, rather than disabling DI validation or composing a database.
rules.why: DI validation stays on and the test stays free of persistence, while a call to the dependency still fails loudly.
rules.check: Look for `ValidateOnBuild = false`/`ValidateScopes = false` or a full database setup in tests that only check registration.

rules.statement: In a test project, prove that composition or option reading constructs no strategy by registering one whose constructor throws.
rules.why: A throwing registration fails the test if the strategy is constructed, which an assertion on the result alone can't show.
rules.check: Look for tests that claim a service is not constructed but only assert on outputs, with no throwing registration.

rules.statement: In a test project, supply configuration that the composition root reads while it registers services with `builder.UseSetting(key, value)`, and assert an effect only that composition has.
rules.why: Configuration added later is not visible while services are registered, and asserting a unique effect makes a value that never arrived fail the test.
rules.check: Look for test factories that add such settings through `ConfigureAppConfiguration` or in-memory collections, or that assert nothing that proves the setting took effect.

rules.statement: In a test project, a test that needs a setup to have taken effect asserts something only that setup produces (for example that a token is a five-segment JWE), so missing setup fails the test.
rules.why: Otherwise the test can pass when the setup never arrived.
rules.check: Look for tests that configure a key, setting or seed and then assert only results that would also hold without it.

rules.statement: In a test project, when seeding a precondition the API would refuse (such as an unreadable document), first assert the precondition holds, then exercise the behavior under test.
rules.why: Without this, the test can pass on data the server actually reads, so it proves nothing.
rules.check: Look for tests that seed deliberately invalid or unusual state and go straight to the behavior assertion without confirming the state.

rules.statement: In a test project, build stored payloads through the production serializer or protector the server uses, never a bare `JsonSerializer` call.
rules.why: The server stores a protected, versioned envelope, so a test with a bare payload passes while the code fails on every stored row.
rules.check: Look for tests that seed persisted payload columns with `JsonSerializer.Serialize(...)` instead of the real persisted-payload serializer or protector.

rules.statement: In a test project, a test method passes `CancellationToken.None` to the test project's own async helpers and leaves a framework call's optional token at its default.
rules.why: The conventions make test cancellation explicit for the project's own methods without cluttering framework calls.
rules.check: Look for test methods passing `default` or a made-up token source to helpers, or adding explicit tokens to calls such as `HttpClient.SendAsync`.

rules.statement: In a test project, an async helper takes a list as `IReadOnlyList<T>` before the trailing `CancellationToken`, never a `params` array, puts no optional parameter before the token, and groups optional inputs in a type with `init` properties.
rules.why: Every caller then passes each input, using a collection expression and `CancellationToken.None`.
rules.check: Look for test helpers with `params` arrays, optional parameters before the `CancellationToken`, or long lists of optional parameters.

rules.statement: In a test project, async helpers return `ValueTask`/`ValueTask<T>`, end in `Async` and take a trailing `CancellationToken` that they pass to every awaited call that accepts one.
rules.why: The test projects follow the same async conventions as production code, and analyzers NCID0002 and NCID0003 enforce it.
rules.check: Analyzer-enforced; a reviewer can skip it.

rules.statement: In a test project, don't ask a member that a framework contract declares (xUnit test methods, `WebApplicationFactory`, `HttpMessageHandler` or `AuthenticationHandler` overrides, `IAsyncDisposable.DisposeAsync`, `IHost`/`IHostedLifecycleService` members, or async lambdas a framework API takes) to return `ValueTask` or take a `CancellationToken`.
rules.why: These members keep the shape of the framework contract they implement.
rules.check: Before reporting a `Task` return type or a missing token, check whether the member overrides or implements a framework contract or is a lambda passed to a framework API.

rules.statement: In a test project, pass `.AsTask()` when handing a `ValueTask` helper's result to an API that takes a `Task`, such as `Task.WhenAll`.
rules.why: The helpers return `ValueTask`, which the `Task`-based combinators don't accept.
rules.check: Look for helpers being changed to return `Task` just so they can be combined with `Task.WhenAll`.

rules.statement: In a test project, an integration test that requests an authorization code sends an S256 PKCE challenge and redeems the code with the matching verifier, as a conforming client does.
rules.why: Codes are bound to an S256 PKCE challenge by default, so a test without it exercises the refusal, not the flow.
rules.check: Look for authorization-endpoint requests in integration tests that have no `code_challenge` and `code_challenge_method=S256`, or token redemptions with no `code_verifier`.

rules.statement: In a test project, reuse the shared helpers for repeated protocol steps (sign-in with the antiforgery exchange, form posts, management-token requests) instead of writing another copy.
rules.why: Copies drift apart from the real flow and from each other.
rules.check: Look for tests that hand-build an antiforgery sign-in, form post or `client_credentials` request where a shared helper already exists.

rules.statement: In a test project, prove equal-time (timing-safe) verification by recording that the hasher or verifier ran on the dummy path, never by measuring elapsed time.
rules.why: Elapsed time is flaky when tests run in parallel.
rules.check: Look for `Stopwatch` or elapsed-time assertions in tests of timing-safe verification.

rules.statement: In a test project, test code that wraps ASP.NET Core Identity's `UserManager<TUser>` against a real `UserManager` composed over EF InMemory as well as against a mocked one.
rules.why: A mocked `UserManager` hides what its own methods do, such as running password validators in `CreateAsync` and rehashing and rotating the security stamp in `CheckPasswordAsync`.
rules.check: Look for adapter tests over `UserManager<TUser>` that only use a mock.

rules.statement: In a test project, write a string literal whose Unicode normalization form matters with escapes (for example `"café"`), never as a pasted character.
rules.why: An editor may normalize a pasted character, which silently changes what the test exercises.
rules.check: Look for literal non-ASCII combining characters or precomposed characters in tests about normalization.

rules.statement: In a test project, assert a redirect URI that the server must deliver exactly as written on `Headers.Location.OriginalString`.
rules.why: `Uri`'s other properties normalize the value, which hides differences from what was written.
rules.check: Look for assertions on `Headers.Location`, `.ToString()` or `.AbsoluteUri` where an exact-as-written URI matters.

rules.statement: In a test project, write a private-use redirect URI as a reverse domain name (`com.example.app:/callback`), not a made-up scheme such as `myapp://callback`.
rules.why: A made-up scheme is of no registered redirect URI kind and is refused.
rules.check: Look for custom-scheme redirect URIs in tests that are not reverse domain names.

rules.statement: In a test project, seed a client registered for the `token_endpoint_auth_method` the test authenticates with, so a negative test is refused for the reason it names.
rules.why: A client registered for another method is refused with `invalid_client` for the mismatch, so the test passes without exercising its rule.
rules.check: Look for negative client-authentication tests whose seeded client's registered method differs from the method used in the request.

rules.statement: In a test project, an end-to-end test of a protocol client routes its named `HttpClient` to the test server's handler and records each exchange, so it proves what goes over the wire as well as the client's result.
rules.why: Checking only the client's result can't show what the client sent, such as a parameter sent twice or a field that should be absent.
rules.check: Look for client-against-host tests that assert only the client's return value when the behavior under test is what goes over the wire.

rules.statement: In a test project, compare a DPoP-bound token's `cnf.jkt` with an RFC 7638 thumbprint computed in the test, and request a new authorization code for each code the test expects to be refused.
rules.why: A thumbprint computed independently proves the binding, and the OP consumes a code before it checks `dpop_jkt`, so a refused code can't be reused.
rules.check: Look for DPoP tests that compare `jkt` with a value taken from the code under test, or that reuse one authorization code across several redemptions expected to be refused.

rules.statement: In a test project, assert a background job's effect by polling with a deadline, not by a fixed delay or a single immediate check.
rules.why: The job runs asynchronously, so a fixed delay is flaky and an immediate check races.
rules.check: Look for `Task.Delay` followed by an assertion, or an immediate assertion on state that a background worker produces.

rules.statement: In a test project, prove a worker's concurrency with a job that waits for a release signal the test controls.
rules.why: A job that waits for a release shows deterministically how many jobs run at once, without depending on timing.
rules.check: Look for concurrency tests that rely on sleeps or timing instead of a gate such as a `TaskCompletionSource` or semaphore.

rules.statement: In a test project, change configuration at runtime through the host's `IConfigurationRoot` (setting values and reloading), not by rebuilding the host.
rules.why: This exercises the reload path the running host actually observes.
rules.check: Look for tests of configuration changes that build a new host or mutate options objects directly.

rules.statement: In a test project, build a certificate subject with `X500DistinguishedNameBuilder` when the string type of each value matters.
rules.why: A subject DN is matched by RFC 4517 rules, not by bytes, so the test must choose each value's string type.
rules.check: Look for subject DNs built from a plain string in tests about DN matching.

rules.statement: In a test project, serve certificate revocation data (CRLs built with `CertificateRevocationListBuilder`, OCSP responses) through a stub HTTP handler, never the network.
rules.why: Tests must not depend on network access or external responders.
rules.check: Look for revocation tests that use a real `HttpClient` or let `X509Chain` fetch revocation data online.

rules.statement: In a test project, pin a protocol encoder or parser to fixture bytes that another implementation (for example OpenSSL) wrote, not only round-trips through our own code.
rules.why: A round-trip through our own encoder and parser can't catch a mistake the two share.
rules.check: Look for encoder or parser tests whose only inputs come from our own encoder.

rules.statement: In a test project, build a JWT with exact or malformed time claims through `IJoseSerializer`, not `IJwtEncoder`.
rules.why: The JWT encoder's `EnsureTokenLifetime` (on by default) injects default `iat`/`nbf`/`exp` and overwrites a non-integer `iat`, so a test of lifetime validation would not get the claims it set.
rules.check: Look for lifetime-validation tests that encode tokens with `IJwtEncoder` while setting absent, malformed or far-off time claims.

rules.statement: In a test project, a test reads its files from the output directory: copy them with `CopyToOutputDirectory` and resolve them from `AppContext.BaseDirectory`, never from a source-relative path such as `[CallerFilePath]`.
rules.why: A CI `ContinuousIntegrationBuild` maps source paths to `/_/`, so a source-relative path exists only on a developer's machine.
rules.check: Look for `[CallerFilePath]`, `CommonDirectoryPath.GetProjectDirectory()` or `../..` walks to locate test files.

rules.statement: In a test project, host a Blazor Web App for an end-to-end test through `WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint>.UseKestrel()` followed by `StartServer()`, not through a `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` in the test process.
rules.why: The factory locates the app's static web assets, which a builder in the test process does not.
rules.check: Look for end-to-end tests that host a Blazor app with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` directly.

rules.statement: In a test project, a browser end-to-end suite shares one collection fixture and gives each test a fresh browser context.
rules.why: Sharing the fixture keeps the expensive setup to one run, and a fresh context keeps cookies and storage from leaking between tests.
rules.check: Look for tests that reuse a browser context or page across tests, or that create per-test fixtures for the hosts.

rules.statement: In a test project, a browser test reads an API response through `fetch` in the page, not by navigating to it, and asserts server-side counters as well as browser outcomes.
rules.why: Firefox shows a JSON response in a viewer, so a navigation to it reads nothing, and browser outcomes alone don't show what the server did.
rules.check: Look for Playwright tests that `GotoAsync` a JSON endpoint and read the page content, or that assert only on the browser.

rules.statement: In a test project, don't treat `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` as the same site in a browser test, and don't treat a port difference as a different site.
rules.why: Browsers treat the two hosts as different sites, while a port never changes a site, which affects `SameSite` cookie behavior.
rules.check: Look for cross-site or same-site cookie assertions that mix `localhost` and `127.0.0.1`, or that rely on ports to make sites differ.
